prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network collapsed to DONE on the first step (episode length 1.0 by 25% of training). I think the hidden rule causes this. Target, missing and extra channels are rolled 4 columns, so the useful target information for an anchor at column x sits at x+4. That is outside the receptive field of two 3x3 convolutions. Every placement therefore looks like it has negative expected reward, and DONE (reward 0) wins. The first fix is to give the network a learned global spatial mixing of the target channels, so it can learn the realignment, while keeping the build stream local. Round 1 tests three things: a full token-mixing realigner, the same network with a recipe giving more updates and samples, and a cheaper factorised row/column mixer applied to both streams. All three raise entropy slightly to slow the collapse to DONE. A 2-seed mean above 0 would already beat the 0.000 baseline.

### Round 2
All four trials so far, the starting network included, score 0. Each one collapses to DONE within 25 to 50% of training. Here is why. The target channels are rolled X/2 = 4 columns, so a 3x3 trunk sees a missing cell 4 columns away from where the brick has to go. Placements therefore look random and lose reward on average, while DONE pays 0. Once the policy settles on DONE, a good single placement would still score above zero, so it could learn from there, but only if the network can line the target up with the build. Round 1 tried to do that with layers that are not translation-equivariant: a full 64x64 cell mix, and an axis mix whose single 8x8 matrix is shared across every channel. Neither learned the shift before the collapse. Giving it more updates (r1c2) only made the collapse come sooner. Next I try a learned, translation-equivariant, circular full-width convolution, so that every cell and every placement teaches the same offset. One candidate applies it only to the target channels, one applies it generically to all channels on both axes, and one raises the entropy bonus to slow the collapse.

### Round 3
The circular (1,X) row convolution is what made the task learnable: all non-circular variants stayed at 0 (DONE at once), all circular ones trained (0.447 target-only, 0.325 generic, 0.339 with entropy 0.05). Seeds for one setting differ by 0.11 to 0.16, so differences among the circular variants are probably noise; higher entropy did not help. Two limits on the best run: (1) training success was still climbing at the end (0.21 at 75%, 0.29 at 100%) and runs used about 65 of 900 s, so more samples look worthwhile; (2) the failures are early DONEs. IoU is 0.885 with almost no wrong cells, and the traces stop with missing cells left, often upper layers. The DONE and value heads only see trunk pooling, which the shift blurs. Missing and extra counts do not change under the shift, so a learned per-cell layer followed by global pooling gives a clean stop signal. Test: more samples, the DONE fix, and both together.

### Round 4
Every trial without a circular row convolution on the target channels scored 0: the agent learned to press DONE at once. The circular (1, X) convolution unlocked learning (r2c1: 0.447). The generic axial version (0.325) and ent_coef 0.05 (0.339) were no better, given the seed noise. Halving PPO epochs from 4 to 2 nearly doubled the samples and gave the clearest gain (r3c1: 0.699, training success still rising at 0.675). So the run is short of samples, not of optimisation per sample. The missing/extra pooling for the DONE head did not help (0.404, and 0.297 with 2 epochs, where one seed scored 0.078). Seed spread is large, up to about 0.44 between seeds. In this final round I push the sample-count lever further, to 1 PPO epoch (about 367k steps), and test a higher learning rate and more frequent smaller updates on top of it. The architecture stays fixed at r3c1, the best so far.

## Trial it ended with
name: 1 epoch, higher lr
hypothesis: Same network as r3c1, with ppo_epochs 1 (about 367k samples) and lr raised from 0.001 to 0.002. One epoch moves the policy less per update; doubling the learning rate makes up for that and speeds the early escape from pressing DONE at once, while the larger sample count is kept. PPO clipping limits instability. Refuted if it scores clearly below the 1-epoch version at lr 0.001, or below r3c1's 0.699 by more than seed noise.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 says: "Target, missing and extra channels are rolled 4 columns, so the useful target information for an anchor at column x sits at x+4." That gives what changes (the target-related channels), the amount (4 columns) and the direction (toward higher x). Round 2 repeats it ("rolled X/2 = 4 columns"), and the circular-convolution fix there matches the wrap-around. The only gap is that it never names the target-height channel.
